title: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
summary: How video LLMs fit long videos into a bounded context: frame sampling, spatial pooling, similarity-based token merging, memory banks, long-context transfer and caption retrieval, with the benchmarks that test them.
outcomes: Compute the visual token cost of a video from frame rate, duration and tokens per frame, and how pooling changes it
Explain why sparse uniform sampling misses short events, and compute the hit probability for N frames
Trace how MovieChat and MA-LMM merge the most similar adjacent frames to keep memory bounded
Compare compression, long-context models (LongVA, Gemini 1.5) and caption retrieval for a given video task
Explain what Video-MME, EgoSchema and LongVideoBench measure and why frame count matters on them

lessons.title: Why an hour of video does not fit: frames times tokens

blocks.md:
You want to ask a model "when did the speaker first show the architecture slide?" about a 1-hour recorded talk. From the image course you know a VLM turns one image into a grid of **visual tokens**, one per patch, and feeds them to the language model like words.

A video is just many images in a row. So the obvious plan is: encode every frame, concatenate all the tokens, and let the language model attend over everything. This lesson shows why that plan breaks, with real numbers.

Start tiny. LLaVA-OneVision ([Li et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03326)) encodes each video frame with a SigLIP encoder into 729 tokens (a 27 x 27 grid), then applies 2 x 2 bilinear interpolation to shrink it to **196 tokens per frame** (a 14 x 14 grid). It samples at most 32 frames per video, so its video input is at most $32 \times 196 = 6{,}272$ tokens.

Now take our talk and sample it at 1 frame per second (fps): 3,600 frames.

blocks.caption: The token budget of a video is a product. Halving either factor halves the cost.

blocks.prompt: A 2 x 2 average pooling on the 14 x 14 grid leaves 7 x 7 = 49 tokens per frame. At 1 fps for one hour, does the video now fit in a 128K-token context window?
blocks.reveal: No. $3600 \times 49 = 176{,}400$ tokens, still above 128K. Spatial pooling cuts cost by exactly 4x, but the frame count (3,600) dominates. At 49 tokens per frame a 128K window holds about 2,612 frames, roughly 44 minutes at 1 fps, and leaves no room for the question or the answer.

scenes.caption: Every frame at 1 fps with 196 tokens each: 705,600 tokens, more than 5 times a 128K context window.
2 x 2 pooling divides tokens per frame by 4 (196 to 49): 176,400 tokens. Better, but still over the window.
LLaVA-OneVision's cap of 32 frames: 6,272 tokens. Fits easily, but one frame now stands for about 112 seconds of video.
Video-LLaVA samples 8 frames uniformly. Costed at the same 196 tokens per frame: 1,568 tokens (450 times fewer than 1 fps). One frame per 7.5 minutes of video.

blocks.md:
That last bar is not a strawman. Video-LLaVA ([Lin et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.10122)) uniformly samples **8 frames** per video, and its own limitations section says this loses detail on long videos. Video-ChatGPT ([Maaz et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05424)) takes more frames but average-pools them hard (lesson 3).

Attention cost makes the problem worse than the token count suggests: self-attention compute grows with the square of sequence length, and the KV cache grows linearly with it.

blocks.title: Where each long-video idea acts in the pipeline

scenes.caption: Naive plan: every frame goes through the encoder and every token reaches the LLM. The budget explodes at the LLM.
Lever 1, sampling: pick fewer frames (uniform or question-aware keyframes). Cheap, but anything between samples is never seen.
Lever 2, compression: pool tokens within a frame, or merge similar tokens across frames.
Lever 3, memory: process frames online and keep a bounded, compressed memory (MovieChat, MA-LMM) instead of all tokens.
Lever 4, change the LLM: extend its context so it accepts far more tokens (LongVA, Gemini 1.5). Lever 5, skip pixels: caption short clips and retrieve text.

blocks.md: Video cost is **frames x tokens per frame**. Every long-video method attacks one factor: fewer frames (sampling), fewer tokens per frame (pooling), fewer tokens over time (merging, memory), a bigger budget (long context), or a different representation (text captions).

blocks.question: A team doubles the frame rate from 1 fps to 2 fps and also switches from 196 to 49 tokens per frame. What happens to the total token count for the same video?
options: It doubles
It halves
It stays the same
It drops to a quarter
blocks.explain: Total = frames x tokens per frame. Frames go up 2x, tokens per frame go down 4x (196 to 49), so the total is 2/4 = 0.5 of the original. More temporal detail can be bought with less spatial detail.

blocks.question: Which statement about 8-frame uniform sampling of a 1-hour video is correct?
options: It is fine because the vision encoder sees all frames before sampling
It costs 8 x 196 = 1,568 visual tokens but leaves 7.5-minute gaps the model never sees
It is equivalent to 1 fps sampling with 2 x 2 pooling
It fails only because the LLM context is too short
blocks.explain: Sampling happens before the encoder, so unsampled frames are never encoded. 3,600 s / 8 = 450 s between samples. The context is not the issue at 1,568 tokens; the missing information is.

lessons.title: Which frames to look at: uniform sampling and the needle problem

blocks.md:
**Uniform sampling** picks $N$ frames evenly spaced over the video, for example one at the middle of each of $N$ equal segments. It needs no knowledge of the question, which is why it is the default in Video-LLaVA (8 frames) and LLaVA-OneVision (up to 32 frames).

The catch: if the answer depends on a short event, such as a slide shown for 5 seconds, uniform sampling only sees it by luck.

scenes.caption: Each cell is a 5-minute stretch of the talk. With 8 frames, samples land at 225 s, 675 s, ... (every 450 s, centered in each segment).
Samples fall in the 0, 10, 15, 25, 30, 40, 45 and 55 minute cells. Four 5-minute stretches contain no frame at all.
The architecture slide is shown from 37:00 to 37:05 (2,220 to 2,225 s), inside the 35-minute cell. The nearest samples are at 2,025 s and 2,475 s: the model never sees it.
Simplified illustration: a question-aware keyframe selector scores many cheap candidate frames against the question and spends its 8-frame budget near the relevant moment.

blocks.md: Let us compute the odds. Suppose an event lasts $L$ seconds and starts at a uniformly random time in a video of length $T$. With a uniform grid of $N$ frames the spacing is $d = T/N$. If $L \ge d$ some frame always lands inside the event; otherwise the chance is the fraction of the spacing the event covers.

blocks.caption: Left: evenly spaced frames. Right: N frames drawn independently at random times. Both ignore edge effects at the start and end of the video.

blocks.prompt: For a 5-second event in a 1-hour video, what is the chance that 8 evenly spaced frames include it? And how many frames guarantee a hit?
blocks.reveal: $P = 5 \times 8 / 3600 \approx 1.1\%$. A guaranteed hit needs spacing of at most 5 s, so $N = 3600 / 5 = 720$ frames. A simulation with 20,000 random event positions agreed with the formula (1.1% at N = 8, 100% at N = 720).

blocks.title: Chance that sampled frames hit a short event

y.label: P(at least one frame inside event)

scenes.caption: Default: a 5-second event in a 1-hour video. The marked points are for these defaults: 8 frames give 1.1%, 64 give 8.9%, 256 give 35.6%.
The grid curve reaches 1 exactly where the frame spacing equals the event length (720 frames). Random times only reach 63.2% there, because random frames clump and leave gaps.
A 60-second event is far easier: 60 frames already guarantee a hit with a grid. Long events forgive sparse sampling; brief ones do not.
A 3-hour video with a 5-second event needs 2,160 evenly spaced frames to guarantee a hit, beyond the plotted range. Longer videos push the requirement up linearly.

blocks.md: A hit is necessary, not sufficient. A sampled frame inside the event only gives the model a chance; it still has to recognize the content at the token resolution it was given. The formula is an upper bound on what sampling allows.

**Keyframe sampling** replaces the blind grid with a choice driven by content. One family scores frames by relevance to the question: Adaptive Keyframe Sampling ([Tang et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.21271)) optimizes both relevance to the prompt and coverage of the whole video under a fixed token budget. Another family is agentic: VideoAgent ([Wang et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.10517)) lets an LLM decide which frames to inspect next, and reports using about 8 frames on average on EgoSchema.

The price is extra computation before the LLM (scoring many candidate frames), and a dependence on the question: a keyframe set picked for one question may be useless for the next.

Production models also treat frame rate as a knob rather than a constant. Qwen2-VL ([Wang et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12191)) samples videos at 2 fps during training and caps a video at 16,384 tokens by lowering per-frame resolution. Qwen2.5-VL ([Bai et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13923)) adds **dynamic FPS** training, so the same model can be fed sparse or dense sampling depending on the video length and budget.

blocks.question: You must answer questions about 2-second events in 30-minute videos and can afford 256 frames. Which statement is right?
options: Uniform sampling hits about 28% of such events, so dense or question-aware selection is needed
Uniform sampling hits every event because 256 frames is a lot
Random sampling would hit more events than a uniform grid
Hit rate does not depend on video length
blocks.explain: $P = \min(1, 2 \times 256 / 1800) \approx 0.284$. A grid always does at least as well as independent random times for the same N, and the hit rate falls as the video gets longer.

blocks.question: Why is question-aware keyframe selection awkward for a chat assistant that answers many follow-up questions about the same video?
options: Keyframes are only defined for videos under one minute
Keyframe selection cannot run on GPUs
Keyframes always contain fewer tokens than uniform frames
The selected frames depend on the question, so each new question may need a new selection pass and new visual tokens
blocks.explain: Relevance is computed against the prompt. A follow-up about a different moment needs different frames, so the encoding and prefill work is redone instead of reusing one cached representation of the video.

lessons.title: Shrinking each frame: spatial pooling, SlowFast and time positions

blocks.md: Sampling decides *which* frames. **Spatial pooling** decides how many tokens each kept frame costs. Average pooling with a $k \times k$ window replaces each $k \times k$ block of neighboring patch tokens by their mean, dividing the token count by $k^2$. Bilinear interpolation (LLaVA-OneVision's 729 to 196) is a smooth variant of the same idea.

blocks.title: 2 x 2 average pooling on a 4 x 4 token grid

scenes.caption: Toy frame: 16 patch tokens, each shown as one activation (real tokens are vectors). Top right holds a tiny detail: one bright patch (0.9) at r1, c3, say a small digit on a slide.
Pooling groups the grid into four 2 x 2 blocks. The top-left block (0.9, 0.7, 0.8, 0.6) is a large uniform object.
After pooling: 4 tokens instead of 16. The large object keeps a strong value (0.75), but the detail's block averages to 0.225: the small digit is diluted by its three blank neighbors.
Cost fell 4x, as in 196 to 49 tokens per frame. The tradeoff: pooling keeps big, uniform regions and washes out small text and small objects.

blocks.md: Pooling can also run over **time**. Video-ChatGPT encodes $T$ frames into a $T \times N$ grid of tokens ($N$ per frame). It averages over space to get $T$ temporal tokens (one per frame) and averages over time to get $N$ spatial tokens, then concatenates them: $T + N$ tokens instead of $T \times N$. LongVA's comparison table lists it at 100 frames and 256 tokens per frame, so 356 tokens instead of 25,600. The cost: averaging over time blurs *when* things happened.

LLaVA-Video ([Zhang et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.02713)) mixes resolutions with a **SlowFast** layout. Every $s$-th frame is a *slow* frame pooled with a $p \times p$ window; the rest are *fast* frames pooled with $2p \times 2p$, so they cost 4 times fewer tokens. Slow frames keep detail, fast frames keep the timeline dense, and the paper reports fitting up to three times more frames than a uniform per-frame budget.

blocks.caption: LLaVA-Video SlowFast budget: T frames, M tokens per frame before pooling, every s-th frame slow.

blocks.md:
Once tokens from many frames sit in one sequence, the LLM must know which frame each came from. Qwen2-VL's **M-RoPE** splits the rotary position into three components: temporal, height and width. Within a frame, height and width ids follow the patch grid; the temporal id increases by one per temporal step. Qwen2-VL also fuses each pair of consecutive frames with a 3D convolution of depth two, so one temporal step covers two frames.

The problem: in Qwen2-VL the temporal id counts frames, not seconds. Qwen2.5-VL aligns the temporal ids to **absolute time**.

blocks.title: Temporal position ids for 8 frames at two sampling rates

scenes.caption: Two clips, 8 frames each, fused in pairs into 4 temporal steps. Clip A is sampled at 2 fps (covers 4 s); clip B at 0.5 fps (covers 16 s). Ids shown relative to the start of the video.
Qwen2-VL style: the temporal id counts steps, 0, 1, 2, 3, for both clips. The model cannot tell a 4-second clip from a 16-second one from positions alone.
Qwen2.5-VL style: id step = tokens_per_second x temporal_patch_size / fps = 2 x 2 / fps. At 2 fps the step is 2, so ids are 0, 2, 4, 6.
At 0.5 fps the step is 8: ids 0, 8, 16, 24. In both clips the id is 2 x seconds, so the gaps between ids encode real time regardless of sampling rate.

blocks.code:
# From Hugging Face transformers, Qwen2.5-VL rope index (simplified)
# config: tokens_per_second = 2, temporal_patch_size = 2
second_per_grid_t = temporal_patch_size / fps     # seconds per temporal step
time_interval = tokens_per_second * second_per_grid_t
t_index = arange(grid_t) * time_interval          # 0, 2, 4, ... at fps = 2
blocks.caption: The released Qwen2.5-VL-7B config sets tokens_per_second to 2, so temporal ids advance 2 per second of video.

blocks.md: With absolute-time ids, a model can answer "what happens at 37:02?" and localize events in seconds even when the sampling rate changed to fit the budget. Qwen2.5-VL's report highlights second-level event localization in videos up to hours long.

blocks.question: A frame grid of 24 x 24 tokens is average-pooled with a 3 x 3 window. How many tokens remain per frame?
blocks.explain: 24 / 3 = 8 per side, so 8 x 8 = 64 tokens, a 9x reduction from 576. Pooling by k x k divides the count by k squared.

blocks.question: Video-ChatGPT keeps T + N tokens by averaging over space and over time separately. Which question is it worst at?
options: What objects appear in the video?
Is the video indoors or outdoors?
Did the person pick up the cup before or after opening the door?
What is the overall topic of the video?
blocks.explain: The N spatial tokens are averaged over all frames, and the T temporal tokens are each one averaged vector per frame. Fine spatial detail tied to a specific moment is blurred, which hurts ordering questions about small actions.

lessons.title: Merging similar frames: MovieChat and MA-LMM memory banks

blocks.md:
Videos are highly redundant: a speaker standing in front of the same slide for 40 seconds produces 40 nearly identical frames. Pooling ignores that; **temporal token merging** exploits it. The rule, inspired by Token Merging (ToMe) for ViTs: measure similarity between temporally adjacent frames, then replace the most similar adjacent pair by their average. Repeat until the budget is met.

Because only adjacent frames merge, temporal order is preserved, and a long static shot collapses into one token set while a quick change survives.

Concrete example. Six frames, each summarized by a 4-dimensional embedding (real frames have hundreds of tokens of thousands of dimensions). Frames 1 to 3 show a slide, frames 4 and 5 show the speaker, frame 6 shows a demo. We want to keep 3 tokens. Similarity is cosine similarity: $\cos(a,b) = \frac{a \cdot b}{\lVert a \rVert \lVert b \rVert}$.

scenes.caption: All pairwise cosine similarities. Two bright blocks appear: frames 1 to 3 (about 0.98 to 0.99) and frames 4 and 5 (0.98). Frame 6 is unlike everything.
Merging only compares neighbors in time, the cells just right of the diagonal: 0.984, 0.990, 0.279, 0.977, 0.342.
The highest adjacent similarity is f2 with f3 (0.990), so they merge first. The low values at f3 to f4 (0.279) and f5 to f6 (0.342) mark scene cuts that should survive.

blocks.title: Greedy merging of 6 frame embeddings into 3

scenes.caption: Six frames, four dimensions each. Merged rows will hold a size-weighted average; absorbed rows are masked.
Step 1: adjacent similarities are 0.984, 0.990, 0.279, 0.977, 0.342. Merge f2 and f3 into their mean [0.825, 0.175, 0.075, 0.15].
Step 2: recompute. f1 to (f2,f3) is now 0.989, still the top. Merge, weighting the pair by its 2 frames: [0.85, 0.15, 0.05, 0.133], the mean of f1, f2, f3.
Step 3: remaining neighbor similarities are 0.284, 0.977, 0.342. Merge f4 and f5 into [0.15, 0.85, 0.25, 0.05]. Three tokens remain.
Result: slide, speaker, demo, in order. The two surviving boundaries have low similarity (0.348 and 0.288), so the scene cuts were kept and the redundancy removed.

blocks.title: Greedy adjacent merging, step by step
blocks.code:
def consolidate(frames, keep):
    sizes = [1] * len(frames)
    while len(frames) > keep:
        sims = [cos(frames[i], frames[i + 1])
                for i in range(len(frames) - 1)]
        k = argmax(sims)
        n = sizes[k] + sizes[k + 1]
        frames[k] = (frames[k] * sizes[k] + frames[k + 1] * sizes[k + 1]) / n
        sizes[k] = n
        del frames[k + 1], sizes[k + 1]
    return frames

scenes.caption: Start with 6 frames and a target of 3 (MovieChat's R_L plays the role of keep).
First pass: compute the five adjacent similarities and pick the largest.
Average f2 and f3 and delete the absorbed frame. Sizes track how many frames each token stands for.
Second pass merges f1 into the (f2,f3) token with weights 1 and 2.
Third pass merges f4 and f5. Length is 3, the loop ends.

blocks.md: **MovieChat** ([Song et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.16449)) wraps this rule in a two-level memory inspired by the Atkinson-Shiffrin model of human memory. Frames are encoded (EVA-CLIP ViT-G/14 plus a BLIP-2 Q-Former, a small transformer whose 32 learned queries cross-attend to the patch features, so each frame becomes 32 tokens) in sliding windows of 16 frames into a **short-term memory**: a fixed buffer of 18 frames. When it fills, the buffer is consolidated by greedy adjacent merging (frame similarity is the average cosine similarity over the 32 tokens) into 2 frames. Those 2 frames are appended to the **long-term memory** (256 frames, so at most $256 \times 32 = 8{,}192$ tokens) and also re-seed the short-term buffer.

scenes.caption: Frames arrive 16 at a time and are encoded into 32 tokens each, then pushed into the short-term buffer.
When the 18-frame buffer is full, it is merged down to 2 representative frames by repeatedly averaging the most similar adjacent pair.
The 2 frames join the long-term memory and re-seed the short-term buffer, which carries context across windows.
Global mode: the question is answered from long-term memory only. Breakpoint mode, for a question about a specific moment, also uses the short-term memory around that moment.

blocks.md:
The payoff is memory use that barely grows with length. MovieChat reports handling videos of more than 10K frames on a 24 GB GPU, while earlier methods it compared against supported around 100 frames.

**MA-LMM** ([He et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.05726)) processes frames online, one at a time, and keeps two banks inside the Q-Former: a **visual memory bank** of past raw frame features and a **query memory bank** of past learned queries, both used as extra keys and values in attention. When a bank exceeds its length $M$, **memory bank compression** computes cosine similarity between temporally adjacent features at each spatial location, and at each location independently averages its most similar adjacent pair, shortening the bank by one. Only the final Q-Former output goes to the LLM, so the LLM input does not grow with video length.

Merging is lossy and question-blind. It removes what *looks* redundant, so a brief, visually small change (a number on a scoreboard updating) can be averaged away before anyone asks about it. MA-LMM's ablation found accuracy saturating at a memory length around 10 to 20 for 100 input frames on its benchmarks; that says those benchmarks are redundant, not that every question is.

blocks.question: A 10-minute static lecture shot is followed by a 3-second cutaway, then the lecture again. With adjacent-similarity merging down to a small budget, what most likely happens?
options: The lecture frames collapse to few tokens while the cutaway survives as its own token
The cutaway is merged first because it is shortest
All frames are merged into one token immediately
The lecture frames are deleted and only the cutaway remains
blocks.explain: Near-identical lecture frames have the highest adjacent similarity, so they merge first. The cutaway has low similarity to both neighbors, so it is merged last, if at all. Merging spends the budget on change.

blocks.question: Why do MovieChat and MA-LMM only merge temporally adjacent frames instead of the globally most similar pair?
options: Global similarity is impossible to compute
Adjacent merging keeps temporal order, so each merged token still stands for one contiguous stretch of time
Adjacent frames are always identical
It makes the LLM context longer
blocks.explain: If the speaker returns to the same slide at minute 5 and minute 50, a global merge would fuse two distant moments into one token and destroy the timeline. Adjacent merging keeps each memory slot contiguous and ordered.

blocks.question: MovieChat's short-term memory holds 18 frames of 32 tokens and consolidates to 2 frames. How many visual tokens does each consolidation add to long-term memory?
blocks.explain: 2 frames x 32 tokens = 64 tokens. The 18 x 32 = 576 tokens in the buffer shrink 9x, and long-term memory is capped at 256 frames, 8,192 tokens.

lessons.title: Bigger context or captions: LongVA, Gemini 1.5, retrieval, benchmarks

blocks.md:
Every method so far shrinks the video to fit the LLM. The opposite approach grows the LLM's context to fit the video.

**LongVA** ([Zhang et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.16852)) takes Qwen2-7B-Instruct and continues pretraining it on **text only** at a 224K context (raising the RoPE base frequency, about 900M tokens). It then does ordinary image-text alignment and instruction tuning on image data only, with no video data at all. The authors call the result **long context transfer**: the long-context skill learned from text carries over to visual tokens.

LongVA's UniRes encoding gives 144 tokens per frame (576 CLIP features per 336 x 336 grid, then 2 x 2 pooling) and treats an $N$-frame video as a very wide image of $N$ grids. The paper reports processing 2,000 frames, more than 200K visual tokens ($2000 \times 144 = 288{,}000$).

To test it the authors built **V-NIAH**, a visual needle-in-a-haystack: a needle image with a question is inserted at different depths of a long haystack video, and the model must answer the question about the needle.

The **Gemini 1.5** report ([Gemini Team, 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.05530)) shows the same strategy at a far larger scale, with a natively multimodal model and contexts up to millions of tokens. In its video haystack test, the text "The secret word is needle" is overlaid on one frame of a long video sampled at 1 fps, and the model is asked for the secret word. Gemini 1.5 Pro found it at every tested depth across the first hour of the AlphaGo documentary, and across 10.5 hours (seven copies concatenated, 37,994 frames, 9.9M tokens). The GPT-4V API in that comparison supported only about the first 3 minutes.

Back-of-envelope from the report's own numbers: a 45-minute film was 2,674 frames at 1 fps and 684k tokens, about 256 tokens per frame. At that rate one hour at 1 fps is about 920K tokens, which is why hour-long video needs a context near a million tokens.

scenes.caption: The report's 1H-VideoQA benchmark, run zero-shot. Frames are linearly subsampled from 1 fps. With 16 frames both models do poorly (36.5% and 45.2%).
With 150 frames both improve (52.3% and 56.3%). More frames means more chances to see the evidence, as the needle formula predicted.
Feeding every frame at 1 fps lifts Gemini 1.5 Pro to 72.2%. The GPT-4V API could not take the full video in that setup.

blocks.md: Needle tests are a floor, not a ceiling. Finding one overlaid word proves the model *can* retrieve from a long context; it does not prove it can reason over many scattered events, count, or order them. That is why the realistic benchmarks below matter more than a green haystack plot.

The third route skips visual tokens in the LLM entirely. **LLoVi** ([Zhang et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.17235)) runs a captioner over short clips (0.5 to 8 s) densely sampled from the video, then gives the captions to an LLM, prompting it to summarize them before answering. It reported 50.3% on EgoSchema, 18.1 points above the previous best at the time. With an index, the same captions support **retrieval**: embed each caption and fetch only the clips relevant to the question.

To see the cost, assume (our assumption, not a paper's) 5-second clips and about 20 text tokens per caption: one hour becomes 720 captions, about 14,400 tokens.

scenes.caption: Offline, once per video: caption every short clip and store the text with its timestamp. Cost is paid at indexing time, not per question.
Per question: retrieve the few captions that match and give only those to the LLM. A follow-up question reuses the same index.
Agentic variants such as VideoAgent let the LLM request a closer look at chosen frames with a VLM when the captions are not enough.
The weak point: anything the captioner did not write down (a number on screen, a subtle gesture) is lost before the question is known.

blocks.md:
How are these compared? Three benchmarks recur:

- **Video-MME** ([Fu et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.21075)): 900 videos (254 hours), 2,700 expert-written multiple-choice questions, split into short (under 2 min), medium (4 to 15 min) and long (30 to 60 min), with optional subtitles and audio.
- **EgoSchema** ([Mangalam et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.09126)): over 5,000 five-way questions on 3-minute egocentric clips. Its *temporal certificate* is the minimum set of subclips a human needs to verify the answer; the median is about 100 seconds. At release, models scored below 33% (random is 20%) and humans about 76%.
- **LongVideoBench** ([Wu et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.15754)): 3,763 videos up to an hour, 6,678 *referring reasoning* questions that point to a specific moment and then ask about it.

LongVideoBench's finding ties the course together: for videos over 180 seconds, GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro gained more than 10% when given 256 frames instead of 16, while the open-source models tested did not improve beyond 16 frames. More frames only help if the model can actually use the longer context.

Choose by the question. Sparse sampling plus pooling suits gist questions. Merging and memory banks suit streaming and bounded memory. Long context gives the most faithful view at the highest cost. Caption retrieval is cheapest per question and reuses work across questions, but only knows what the captioner wrote.

blocks.question: A support team asks many questions about the same 2-hour screen recording, often about exact error codes shown briefly on screen. Which design fits best?
options: 8 uniformly sampled frames with 2 x 2 pooling
Caption retrieval over 5-second clips alone, since captions are cheap
Index the clips once, retrieve candidate moments per question, then re-inspect those frames at full resolution with a VLM
MovieChat global mode with a 256-frame long-term memory
blocks.explain: Many questions favor a reusable index. Brief, small on-screen text is exactly what pooling, merging and generic captions lose, so the retrieved moments need a full-resolution second look.

blocks.question: A model scores 100% on a video needle-in-a-haystack test at 1 hour. What can you conclude?
options: It will answer any question about hour-long videos correctly
It can locate a single salient item anywhere in an hour of context; multi-event reasoning still needs benchmarks like Video-MME or LongVideoBench
Its frame sampling is uniform
It uses a memory bank
blocks.explain: A needle test isolates retrieval of one planted item. Real questions require combining several moments, ordering and counting, which is what the long splits of Video-MME and LongVideoBench's referring reasoning test.

sources.label: LongVA: Long Context Transfer from Language to Vision (Zhang et al., 2024)
